storySeeds.title: Orion: one family, born in waves
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Do stars have families, and do they all grow up at once?
storySeeds.summary: Start at Meissa’s exposed 5-Myr cluster, drop to the Orion Nebula where θ¹ Ori C is still lighting its 1-Myr cloud, then ι Ori (the likely slingshot that launched AE Aur and μ Col), σ Orionis (a weighed multiple at the heart of its own young cluster), the Belt siblings, and close on Betelgeuse: what heavy stars like these become. Optional coda: point binoculars at AE Aur in Auriga, a runaway sibling.

storySeeds.title: Two clusters and an impostor
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: How can you tell the age of a star family, and who really belongs to it?
storySeeds.summary: Blue-white Pleiades (125 Myr; Pleione’s changing disk as a side note) → Hyades five times older, where θ¹ Tau has become a giant while its same-age sibling θ² is still white → ε Tau, first cluster star with a planet → twist: Aldebaran, the bright orange ‘member’, is a foreground star at less than half the distance. Challenge extension: T Tauri, a star still being born, 1½° from ε Tau.

storySeeds.title: Red, redder, reddest: where your carbon comes from
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: Why are some stars red, and is red always the same thing?
storySeeds.summary: Rigel (12,100 K) and Bellatrix set the hot end; Betelgeuse (3,600 K) the cool, oxygen-rich end; then the carbon stars W Ori and Hind’s Crimson Star (≈2,400–2,700 K), reddened by carbon they dredged up, with Arneb as a distance twist on the way. Payoff: some of the carbon in you was made in giants like R Lep. R Lep is volatile: use W Ori if R Lep is near minimum.

storySeeds.title: Auriga: hidden companions and a runaway
storySeeds.drivingQuestion: How do we learn about stars we cannot see?
storySeeds.summary: Capella’s two giants weighed by their 104-day orbit → ε Aurigae, eclipsed every 27 years by a dark disk imaged in 2010 → ζ Aurigae, a supergiant hiding a hot star every 972 days → Menkalinan’s shallow 4-day eclipses → AE Aurigae, a runaway thrown out of Orion 2.5 Myr ago → the clusters of Auriga as a coda.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine almost everything around it?
card.answer: That is the whole trick: a dim glow spread over an almost absurd amount of surface still adds up to far more light than the Sun will ever give.
card.glance: A bright orange-red star on Orion’s shoulder, whose color blooms when you nudge the focus slightly off.
card.whyHere: Betelgeuse is what a heavy star looks like near the end of its life, a cool, swollen giant on Orion’s shoulder.
card.see: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s eastern shoulder, the bright orange star opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red suddenly becomes obvious; swing to Rigel to feel the contrast. Its brightness drifts over months, so judge it fresh each time.
card.understand: A star’s color is a thermometer, and Betelgeuse’s says its surface is only about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so each square meter of it shines more feebly than the Sun’s. The surprise is how many square meters there are. Astronomers timed its slow pulsations and fed them into models of how heavy stars age, and out came about 18 Suns’ worth of matter swollen to some 760 times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
card.connect: Heavy stars like this do not fade quietly, and the wreckage of one that already exploded lies next door in Taurus.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s VLT pictures show its blotchy surface and the 2019–20 dimming; binoculars and ordinary photos show only a point.
card.notSee: Its disk and surface spots: these need the largest telescopes and interferometers.
card.deeper: Joyce et al. (2020) combined its pulsation periods with evolution models: 16.5–19 solar masses, about 764 solar radii and 168 (+27/−15) parsecs, early in core-helium burning, so the supernova is most likely about 100,000 years away. During the 2020 Great Dimming, Levesque & Massey measured 3,600 ± 25 K, far too small a cooling to explain the fade; VLT imaging then showed a dust veil over its southern half (Montargès et al. 2021).

card.question: How does Rigel, a hundred times farther than Sirius, manage to look almost as bright?
card.answer: Rigel pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun’s light, which is how it rivals nearby Sirius from a hundred times farther away.
card.glance: A brilliant blue-white star at Orion’s foot, diagonally across from orange Betelgeuse.
card.whyHere: Rigel sits at the hot end of the stellar thermometer, and it is the sky’s best lesson that how bright a star looks says little about how bright it is.
card.see: Rigel is Orion’s foot, the brilliant blue-white star diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Hold it in the field and its icy color is unmistakable, especially just after a look at the orange shoulder. A faint companion sits very close, but binoculars lose it in the glare.
card.understand: Its color says the surface is about 12,000 K, twice as hot as the Sun’s, glowing the way metal does when heated past red and yellow. Its distance comes from parallax: as Earth circles the Sun, Rigel shifts against far more distant stars by a few thousandths of an arcsecond, and the Hipparcos satellite caught that tiny wobble well enough to put it about 860 light-years away. Light fades with the square of distance, so anything this bright from that far must be extraordinary.
card.wonder: The light reaching you tonight left Rigel in the 12th century, while stone castles were rising across medieval Europe.
card.connect: Brightness fooled you here, and not far away a dazzling star owes its glare mostly to living next door.
card.photoCaption: Any photo of Rigel is dominated by glare and diffraction spikes; the spikes come from the telescope, not the star.
card.deeper: The Hipparcos parallax (3.78 ± 0.34 mas) gives about 860 light-years with a ±9% spread. Przybilla et al. (2006) derived 12,100 ± 150 K from non-LTE modeling of its spectrum. A fit to its spectral energy distribution gives roughly 80,000 times the Sun’s luminosity (McDonald et al. 2012), uncertain by about 20% because it scales with the distance squared. Stars this luminous usually end as core-collapse supernovae.

card.question: Does Aldebaran really belong to the V-shaped cluster it seems to lead?
card.answer: So Aldebaran is a passer-by in the family portrait: at about 67 light-years it stands less than halfway to the cluster and simply lines up in front of it from where we stand.
card.glance: A bright orange star at one tip of the V-shaped Hyades, the face of Taurus the Bull.
card.whyHere: Every family photo has someone who wandered into the frame, and in the Hyades that someone is the brightest star of all.
card.see: Aldebaran is the orange eye of Taurus, at one tip of the V of the Hyades. Frame the whole V and its warm orange stands apart from the white and pale-yellow cluster stars; then glance south-east to Betelgeuse and ask yourself which of the two is redder.
card.understand: Aldebaran is an orange giant, a star that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width. We know its size because the Moon sometimes passes in front of it, and the light fades out over a fraction of a second instead of switching off at once. Its distance comes from parallax, the small yearly shift the Hipparcos satellite measured against faraway stars, and the Hyades, measured the same way, turn out to lie more than twice as far.
card.wonder: Aldebaran’s light left around 1960 and the cluster’s in the 1870s, so a single binocular field holds two different eras.
card.connect: Betelgeuse, just to the south-east, shows how differently a much heavier star grows old.
card.photoCaption: Photos make it look embedded in the cluster; only distance measurements reveal the gap.
card.deeper: Heiter et al. (2015) adopted 3,927 ± 40 K from its angular diameter and total flux. A lunar-occultation diameter of 20.58 milliarcseconds (Richichi & Roccatagliata 2005) combined with the Hipparcos distance gives about 45 solar radii. Gaia-era studies put the Hyades center about 154 light-years away (Hunt & Reffert 2024), so Aldebaran stands roughly 87 light-years in front of the cluster.

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.whyHere: Capella looks like one golden star, yet it is two giants in a tight embrace, and the way they were weighed is a small masterpiece.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows one bright point; only interferometers have resolved the two giants.
card.deeper: Torres et al. (2015) combined spectroscopy and interferometry: 2.57 and 2.48 solar masses, radii of 12.0 and 8.8 solar radii, and temperatures of about 4,970 and 5,730 K. Models fit only if the cooler, heavier star is already in its helium-burning (red clump) phase while its companion is still crossing toward the giant branch.

card.question: Why is Sirius the brightest star in the night sky?
card.answer: Sirius is a fairly ordinary star that simply lives next door, so close that its light reaches you in under nine years.
card.glance: A blazing white point below and left of Orion’s Belt, flashing color when low.
card.whyHere: Sirius is the most dazzling star of the night, and the reason is so ordinary it is almost a letdown, until you meet its tiny companion.
card.see: Orion’s Belt, followed down and to the left, points straight at Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers red, green and blue, but that is our turbulent air, not the star. Park it near the edge of the binocular field to tame the glare, which also hides its faint companion.
card.understand: Sirius has about twice the Sun’s mass and a surface near 9,900 K, so it burns pure white, but plenty of stars are hotter and heavier. What sets it apart is its parallax: it shifts against the background more than almost any other bright star, which puts it only 8.6 light-years away. Every 50 years it is circled by Sirius B, a white dwarf, the bare cooling core a star leaves when it dies, and two decades of Hubble images of that orbit weighed both stars.
card.wonder: Sirius B holds about a Sun’s worth of matter in a ball the size of Earth, so a teaspoon of it would weigh tons.
card.connect: Another winter star lets you see a white dwarf for yourself, with nothing more than steady binoculars.
card.photoCaption: Hubble had to overexpose Sirius A to show Sirius B at all; no binocular or small telescope can.
card.notSee: Sirius B. Only Hubble-class images or large telescopes in perfect seeing show it.
card.deeper: Bond et al. (2017) combined two decades of Hubble images with about 2,300 historical measurements: Sirius A has 2.063 ± 0.023 and Sirius B 1.018 ± 0.011 solar masses in a 50.13-year orbit, and models give Sirius A an age of about 240 million years. VLTI interferometry measured Sirius A’s diameter as 1.711 times the Sun’s (Kervella et al. 2003). The Hipparcos parallax, 379.21 ± 1.58 mas, puts the system 8.6 light-years away.

card.question: What is a star like Procyon about to become?
card.answer: Procyon is about to swell into a giant and, much later, shrink into a white dwarf, and since its companion has already made that whole trip, the bright star’s future is orbiting right beside it.
card.glance: A bright, creamy-white star, the third corner of the triangle it makes with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
card.whyHere: Procyon is a neighbor at a turning point: its long, steady adult life is ending, and the dead star circling it shows where that road leads.
card.see: Procyon is the eastern corner of the Winter Triangle, with Sirius and Betelgeuse. Compare it with Sirius to the south and it looks a touch warmer, creamy rather than icy white. Then sweep 4° north-west to fainter, blue-white Gomeisa for contrast.
card.understand: Procyon has about one and a half times the Sun’s mass and lies only 11 light-years away. Its faint companion, Procyon B, circles it every 41 years, and Hubble’s patient tracking of that orbit weighed both stars. Procyon’s diameter, measured directly with an interferometer, came out at about twice the Sun’s, a little too large for a star still comfortably burning hydrogen, and its gentle oscillations agree that the core is nearly spent.
card.wonder: Procyon B packs six-tenths of the Sun’s mass into a ball about the size of Earth.
card.connect: An orange giant in Gemini shows the next chapter: a star that has already finished swelling.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single bright point; Procyon B needs Hubble.
card.deeper: Bond et al. (2015) used two decades of Hubble images to measure 1.478 ± 0.012 (Procyon A) and 0.592 ± 0.006 (Procyon B) solar masses in a 40.84-year orbit, and models then give Procyon A an age of about 2.7 billion years. VLTI interferometry measured its diameter as 2.05 solar diameters (Kervella et al. 2004); together with its oscillations this marks a star finishing its hydrogen-burning life.

card.question: What could block a star’s light for almost two years?
card.answer: It is a vast, dark, tilted disk of dust, many times wider than Earth’s orbit and probably hiding a smaller star inside, that slides across the bright star once every 27 years.
card.glance: A modest star at the top of the Kids, the small triangle just south of Capella in Auriga.
card.whyHere: Every 27 years something huge and dark slides in front of ε Aurigae, and it took astronomers nearly two centuries to get a look at it.
card.see: From Capella, drop a few degrees south to the thin triangle of the Kids; ε Aurigae is the brightest of the three. Between eclipses it looks unremarkable, a steady white point. Its neighbor ζ Aurigae, the western star of the lower pair, has eclipses of its own every two and a half years.
card.understand: ε Aurigae is an eclipsing binary, a pair whose orbit, seen edge-on, carries one member in front of the other. The puzzle was the eclipse itself: it lasts almost two years, so whatever passes in front must be enormous, yet it gives off almost no light of its own. During the 2009 to 2011 eclipse, interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, finally caught the culprit in silhouette.
card.wonder: The next eclipse should begin around 2036–37, so there is still time to get to know the star before it happens.
card.connect: Its neighbor in the Kids hides a different eclipse, one you wait out in weeks rather than decades.
card.photoCaption: The disk was imaged in infrared with the CHARA interferometer; no ordinary photograph can show it.
card.deeper: Kloppenborg et al. (2010) reconstructed CHARA interferometer images during the 2009–2011 eclipse: an opaque, tilted disk crossing the F-type star, evidence that the bright star is not a massive supergiant after all. GCVS gives a 9,884-day period and a 2.92–3.88 V range. Its distance is genuinely uncertain: Hipparcos, Gaia DR2 and Gaia EDR3 parallaxes disagree by factors of two, because the star is too bright and too variable for the satellites to measure well.

card.question: What makes the Orion Nebula glow?
card.answer: When the electrons fall back, the hydrogen glows in its own particular colors like a neon sign, and this one system supplies most of the ultraviolet that keeps the sign lit; switch it off and most of the nebula would go dark.
card.glance: One bright point inside the glowing heart of the Orion Nebula, in Orion’s Sword.
card.whyHere: Every glowing cloud needs a power source, and the Orion Nebula’s is hidden in plain sight inside its brightest knot.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula, the fuzzy middle star of the Sword below the Belt, and look at the bright knot in its core. Binoculars merge the four Trapezium stars into one point, and θ¹ Orionis C is the brightest of them.
card.understand: θ¹ Orionis C is a young pair of very heavy stars, together about 44 times the Sun’s mass. That weight comes from watching the two swing through their closest approach with an infrared interferometer and applying the same orbital laws that weigh the planets. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot, and they flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light energetic enough to tear electrons off hydrogen atoms.
card.wonder: It is only about a million years old: when it began to shine, our ancestors were already walking upright.
card.connect: Not every star born here stays home, and one of the Trapezium’s siblings was flung all the way into Auriga.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split the Trapezium into four stars; binoculars show one point inside the glow.
card.notSee: The separate Trapezium stars, which need a telescope at about 30× or more.
card.deeper: Kraus et al. (2009) followed the C1–C2 pair through periastron with infrared interferometry and derived a combined mass of about 44 solar masses. The distance is that of the Orion Nebula Cluster, 414 ± 7 pc from VLBA radio parallaxes (Menten et al. 2007), and the cluster age is roughly 0.3–2 million years (Hillenbrand 1997).

card.question: How do you weigh a star a thousand light-years away?
card.answer: You watch something orbit it, because an orbit’s size and period pin down the mass inside; for Alnitak they give at least about 14 Suns, and more if it lies as far away as the rest of the Belt.
card.glance: The left-hand star of Orion’s Belt, brilliant blue-white.
card.whyHere: Alnitak belongs to Orion’s young family of hot, heavy stars, and it is one of the few of its kind weighed directly rather than estimated.
card.see: Fit all three Belt stars in one field, then center Alnitak at the eastern end. Just south of it lies the Horsehead region, but binoculars show only stars there; the dark horse needs a telescope and a filter.
card.understand: Alnitak is a supergiant of the hottest kind, with a close partner that circles it every seven years. Astronomers followed that partner around a full orbit with an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, measuring how far apart the two appear on the sky, while spectra clocked how fast each moves toward and away from us. Put the angle and the speed together and you get both the true size of the orbit and a distance of about 960 light-years, closer than the 1,250 light-years measured for its Belt neighbor Alnilam, a disagreement not yet settled.
card.wonder: Its light set out around the 11th century, when William the Conqueror crossed to England.
card.connect: Its Belt neighbor Alnilam looks just as bright, and it weighs about twice as much.
card.photoCaption: Wide photos show the Flame and Horsehead nebulae beside Alnitak; binoculars show the star alone.
card.notSee: The Flame and Horsehead nebulae: telescope and camera targets.
card.deeper: Hummel et al. (2013) followed the Aa–Ab pair with the Navy Precision Optical Interferometer over its full seven-year orbit and combined it with spectroscopy: 14.0 ± 2.2 and 7.4 ± 1.1 solar masses at 294 ± 21 pc. A photometric distance from the B companion gives 387 ± 54 pc, so the distance is still debated. Brown et al. (1994) dated the Belt subgroup, Orion OB1b, to about 1.7 million years, but models of its brightest member, Alnilam, give 4.5 (Zsargó et al. 2020) to 5.7 million years (Voss et al. 2010).

ageMyr.note: 4.47 Myr (Zsargó+2020); 5.7 Myr (Voss+2010); replaces Brown+1994's OB1b subgroup age of 1.7 Myr, too young for a supergiant of about 28 M☉

card.question: How fast can a giant star spin before it starts to come apart?
card.answer: Very nearly as fast as it can: though about 28 times wider than the Sun, Alnilam turns once in about four days, close to the point where its equator would start to fling gas away.
card.glance: The middle star of Orion’s Belt, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.whyHere: Alnilam, the middle of Orion’s Belt, is a young blue supergiant that turns out not to be round.
card.see: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. A curving string of fainter stars winds through the Belt, and many of them were born in the same burst of star formation.
card.understand: Alnilam is a blue supergiant, one of the biggest and most luminous kinds of star, about 28 Suns in mass. In 2025 astronomers measured its shape with the interferometer of ESO’s Very Large Telescope and found it is not round: its equator bulges outward, the signature of fast rotation. The same work gave a surface near 25,000 K and a distance of about 1,250 light-years, much closer than older estimates, which makes the star less extreme than once thought.
card.wonder: Alnilam spins fast enough to bulge at its equator, while the much smaller Sun takes almost a month to turn once.
card.connect: Rigel, at Orion’s foot, shares the same blue-white color but sits a few hundred light-years closer.
card.photoCaption: Photos show Alnilam inside faint reddish nebulosity that binoculars do not reveal.
card.deeper: Oplištilová et al. (2025) combined VLTI interferometry with spectroscopy: 384 ± 8 pc, 27.6 ± 1.5 solar radii, 28.4 ± 2.0 solar masses, about 25,000 K and a rotation period near 4.3 days, close to critical. Older studies that assumed the Hipparcos distance of about 600 pc made it far more luminous and massive, a reminder that a star’s power is only as reliable as its distance.

distanceLy.note: adopts the Collinder 69 cluster distance, dist50 393.8 pc (Gaia DR3)

card.question: Where did the cloud that made Orion’s head go?
card.answer: The fierce light of its hot young stars, and probably that supernova, swept the leftover gas outward into a huge ring, leaving this family standing in the open.
card.glance: The head of Orion: a tight little triangle of stars where you expect a single one.
card.whyHere: Meissa is the hot heart of a young star family at Orion’s head, sitting in strangely empty space.
card.see: Point at Orion’s head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn the faint naked-eye smudge into a compact triangle with a dozen fainter stars around it. The ring of gas shows only in long-exposure photos.
card.understand: Meissa belongs to the hottest class of stars and sits at the center of a young cluster called Collinder 69. Gaia’s measurements of more than a thousand members show a family about five million years old, all at the same distance. Around them lies a broken ring of gas and dust, and when astronomers reconstructed the region’s history they found signs that a star near the center exploded as a supernova, the death of a heavy star, and drove the leftover gas outward.
card.wonder: Meissa's young family blew a ring of gas so wide that in long-exposure photographs it frames the whole head of Orion.
card.connect: Down in Orion’s Sword, a younger family is still wrapped in its cloud.
card.photoCaption: Wide-field photos show a big reddish ring around Orion’s head; binoculars show only the stars.
card.notSee: The λ Orionis ring of glowing gas.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) place Collinder 69 at 394 pc, about 5 (3.4–7.0) million years old, with over 1,200 Gaia members. Dolan & Mathieu (2002) reconstructed the history of the λ Orionis region and argued that a recent supernova near the center drove the remaining gas into the present molecular ring. Meissa itself is a 3″ double that needs a telescope.

teffK.note: median of 7 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2023A&A...671A..36A 33,200 K; 2018A&A...613A..65H 34,500 K)

historyHook.text: Traced backwards, AE Aurigae and μ Columbae were together in the young Trapezium cluster in Orion about 2.5 million years ago.

card.question: How did a star born in Orion end up in Auriga?
card.answer: A close encounter between two pairs of heavy stars threw it out, sending AE Aurigae one way and μ Columbae the other like billiard balls after the break, and leaving ι Orionis behind as the battered survivor.
card.glance: A plain-looking star in Auriga, easy in binoculars, with a remarkable past.
card.whyHere: AE Aurigae is a heavy young star sitting far from any nursery, and its path across the sky is a detective story told backward.
card.see: Start at the star cluster M38 in Auriga and drift about 3° west-south-west to the lone brighter star there. Nothing about it looks unusual; the Flaming Star Nebula it lights up is a target for cameras.
card.understand: Stars drift slowly across the sky, and satellites measure that drift precisely. Run AE Aurigae’s motion backward and it meets another runaway, μ Columbae, which is racing the opposite way. Both paths converge on the young Trapezium cluster in Orion about 2.5 million years ago, and at the same spot sits a third suspect: ι Orionis, a tight pair of heavy stars on a stretched orbit.
card.wonder: The Flaming Star Nebula that it lights up is not its birth cloud at all, just one it happens to be plowing through.
card.connect: Its birthplace, the Orion Nebula, is still making stars like it tonight.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the red and blue Flaming Star Nebula (IC 405) around it; binoculars do not.
card.deeper: Hoogerwerf, de Bruijne & de Zeeuw (2001) retraced Hipparcos and radio astrometry: AE Aur, μ Col and the eccentric binary ι Ori occupied a very small volume about 2.5 Myr ago, consistent with ejection from the nascent Trapezium cluster in a binary–binary encounter (an idea going back to Blaauw & Morgan 1954). Gaia EDR3 puts AE Aur about 1,270 light-years away.

ageMyr.note: σ Orionis cluster age 3 ± 1 Myr as commonly adopted

multiplicity.systemNote: Aa–Ab and A–B are interferometric; E (42″) is a binocular split, D (13.5″) a challenge.

card.question: How many stars hide in the single point of σ Orionis?
card.answer: At least three heavy stars are bound together in the central point, with more stars around them, and the central pair’s orbit pins the young cluster’s distance at about 1,260 light-years with rare precision.
card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the left-hand Belt star.
card.whyHere: σ Orionis sits at the heart of its own young cluster below the Belt, and its stars are some of the best-weighed heavy stars known.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; a closer one due east, and many more, need a telescope.
card.understand: The central pair is far too close for any ordinary telescope, but interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, have traced its orbit. Combine the size of that orbit on the sky with spectra that clock the stars’ speeds, and you get masses of about 17 and 13 Suns. The distance comes as a bonus, because the orbit’s true size in kilometers and its apparent size in arcseconds can only match at one distance.
card.wonder: Around the bright star swarm dozens of faint brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen, born from the same cloud.
card.connect: The same young family stretches along the Belt just above.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split σ Orionis into a sparkling multiple; binoculars show one bright star with one or two companions.
card.deeper: Schaefer et al. (2016) resolved the inner Aa–Ab orbit with CHARA, NPOI and VLTI: 16.99 ± 0.20 and 12.81 ± 0.18 solar masses, B at 11.5 ± 1.2, and an orbital-parallax distance of 387.5 ± 1.3 pc. Simón-Díaz et al. (2015) found the inner pair’s model ages younger than the 3 ± 1 million years usually adopted for the cluster. WDS lists E at 42″ and D at 13.5″.

distanceLy.note: Pleiades cluster distance, dist50 134.8 pc (Gaia DR3)

periodDays.note: orbital period of the companion (Hα radial velocities)

card.question: Why does Pleione’s brightness keep changing over the years?
card.answer: As the disk tilts, tears and rebuilds, the amount of glowing gas we see changes, and the star’s brightness rises and falls with it over decades.
card.glance: A fainter star tucked tight against Atlas, on the eastern edge of the Pleiades.
card.whyHere: Pleione is the Pleiad that will not keep still, its brightness drifting over the decades.
card.see: Find Atlas at the eastern end of the Pleiades dipper. Pleione sits just north of it, so close that the naked eye merges the two, but binoculars split them easily. Over months and years its brightness slowly changes, so compare it with Atlas each season.
card.understand: Pleione is a hot young star rotating so fast that gas flows off its equator into a flat, glowing disk. The disk shows up in the spectrum as bright hydrogen light, and that light betrays a companion too, shifting back and forth every 218 days as the companion swings around. Spectra gathered over many years suggest the companion’s pull slowly tips the disk until the strain tears it apart.
card.wonder: One model has the disk tilting by about 30° over 34 years before the companion’s pull rips it in two.
card.connect: Other spinning stars with disks shine in the winter sky, and one sits right beside the Crab Nebula.
card.photoCaption: Photos show it merged with Atlas and the blue haze of the Pleiades; its disk is far too small to image.
card.deeper: Nemravová et al. (2010) found a 218.025-day orbital period in the Hα emission, confirming a companion. Marr et al. (2022) modeled Hα spectra from 2005–2019 and proposed a disk that tilts by about 30° over 34 years and is then torn by the companion’s tides. As a Pleiades member it shares the cluster’s distance, about 440 light-years.

eventDependent.note: Its disk comes and goes over decades; brightness (about 4.8–5.5) and color cannot be predicted offline.

distanceLy.note: Pleiades cluster distance, dist50 134.8 pc (Gaia DR3)

teffK.note: median of 1 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2001A&A...378..861C 13,490 K; only one entry, treat as approximate)

lumLsun.note: SED fit at 123.6 pc gives 1,160 L☉; about 1,400 L☉ at the Gaia cluster distance

card.question: How can a cluster’s brightest star tell you its age?
card.answer: Alcyone is among the heaviest Pleiades still shining, and that cutoff dates the family to about 125 million years, an age confirmed independently by the lithium left in its faintest members.
card.glance: The brightest of the Pleiades, at the junction of the little dipper’s bowl and handle.
card.whyHere: Alcyone leads the sky’s most famous star family, and the fact that it still shines blue-white turns out to be a clock.
card.see: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle, where the little dipper’s bowl meets its handle. Every bright member shares its blue-white color, a family resemblance. Count how many fainter siblings binoculars add to the naked-eye six or seven.
card.understand: Alcyone is a hot star with a surface around 13,000 K, roughly a thousand times as luminous as the Sun. All the Pleiades formed from one cloud at the same time, but heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so the heaviest members have already run out. It works like a row of candles of different lengths lit together: the shortest one still burning tells you how long ago they were lit.
card.wonder: When the Pleiades were born, dinosaurs had already walked the Earth for about a hundred million years.
card.connect: A family five times older sits right next door, and its brightest members have already turned orange.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures wrap Alcyone in blue dust; binoculars show crisp blue-white stars.
card.deeper: The cluster distance, 134.8 pc, is the Gaia DR3 value of Hunt & Reffert (2024); the lithium-depletion age is 125 ± 8 million years (Stauffer et al. 1998). Alcyone’s luminosity comes from a spectral-energy-distribution fit (McDonald et al. 2012) at a slightly smaller distance, so treat it as approximate. The blue haze in photos belongs to an unrelated dust cloud the cluster is passing through.

card.question: Why do two stars born together look so different?
card.answer: θ¹ simply started out a little heavier and reached old age first, so its white sibling shows how it looked not so very long ago.
card.glance: A naked-eye pair in the Hyades V: a white star beside a yellow-orange giant.
card.whyHere: The two θ Tauri stars are siblings of the same age that look nothing alike, and that difference is the key to reading a cluster’s age.
card.see: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair that binoculars split at a glance. θ² is white and θ¹ yellow-orange, and a slight defocus makes the contrast stronger.
card.understand: Both stars were born in the Hyades about 625 million years ago, which we know because they share the cluster’s distance and its motion through space. Yet θ¹ has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant, while θ² is still hot and white, near the end of its long, steady adult life. A star only a little heavier burns its fuel a lot faster, so a small difference at birth puts siblings in different chapters.
card.wonder: θ² is the brightest true member of the Hyades, since brighter Aldebaran only pretends to belong.
card.connect: The bright orange star 2° away, Aldebaran, is no sibling at all.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows both stars with their colors; it is how binoculars show them too.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 places θ² at about 150 light-years and θ¹ at about 132, both within the cluster, whose age is about 625 ± 50 million years (Perryman et al. 1998). θ¹ is one of the four classic Hyades red giants, with γ, δ¹ and ε Tauri. Each star of the pair is itself a close binary, unresolvable in binoculars; the wide pair moves with the cluster but is not an orbiting pair.

teffK.note: median of 67 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2022A&A...663A...4S 5,133 K; 2024A&A...691A..53S 5,117 K)

card.question: Can you see a white dwarf with binoculars?
card.answer: Under a dark sky, braced 10×50s can just show one: the faint point beside 40 Eridani is the bare, Earth-sized core of a dead star, still cooling about 16 light-years from your eyepiece.
card.glance: A yellow-orange star in Eridanus; with braced binoculars, a faint companion beside it.
card.whyHere: A white dwarf is what our Sun will become, and 40 Eridani offers a rare chance to see one with your own binoculars.
card.see: Find 40 Eridani about 15° west of Rigel, nearly level with it, a yellow-orange star in Eridanus. Brace the binoculars and look about 1½ arcminutes to its east-south-east for a very faint point at the limit of braced 10×50s under a dark sky: 40 Eri B.
card.understand: 40 Eridani is a triple: a Sun-like star, with a white dwarf and a small red dwarf orbiting each other farther out. Their orbit weighs the white dwarf at just over half the Sun’s mass, yet it is faint and white-hot at once, which means it must be tiny, about the size of Earth. When astronomers first worked that out, the combination looked impossible, and it took the new quantum physics to explain what holds such crushed matter up.
card.wonder: Star Trek fans know the brighter star here as the sun of Spock’s home world, Vulcan.
card.connect: The brightest white dwarf of all hides beside Sirius, lost in its glare.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos show all three stars; in binoculars B is a faint speck and C is invisible.
card.deeper: Mason et al. (2017) revised B’s dynamical mass to 0.573 ± 0.018 solar masses; Bond et al. (2017) showed its temperature and radius then fit carbon–oxygen white-dwarf models with a thin hydrogen layer, giving a cooling age of about 122 million years and a total age of about 1.8 billion years. WDS lists A–BC at 83″ (2024). Gaia EDR3 puts the system 16.3 light-years away.

teffK.note: median of 110 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2024A&A...692A.228C 5,073 K; 2024A&A...683A.125P 5,076 K)

superlatives.claim: one of the nearest stars known to have both a giant planet and a dust belt

card.question: What does a young version of our Solar System look like?
card.answer: It looks much like ε Eridani, a slightly smaller sun with a planet lighter than Jupiter and a cold ring of comet dust, as our own system may once have looked.
card.glance: An unremarkable star in Eridanus with a soft yellow-orange tint.
card.whyHere: ε Eridani is a neighbor only 10.5 light-years away, a younger cousin of the Sun that already has a planet and a ring of comet dust.
card.see: From Zaurak (γ Eridani), move about 7° west-north-west. You pass δ Eridani first, a shade brighter, and ε Eridani is the next star along, about 2½° beyond it; its gentle yellow-orange tint sets it apart. The planet and dust ring are far beyond any amateur telescope, so the eyepiece shows the star and your imagination supplies the rest.
card.understand: ε Eridani is a little smaller, cooler and younger than the Sun, perhaps half a billion to a billion years old. A camera tuned to faint heat rather than light found a ring of cold dust around it, much like our Kuiper belt of icy leftovers beyond Neptune. The planet was harder to catch, because it never shows itself; it only makes the star sway toward and away from us, and 30 years of patient spectra traced that sway around a seven-year orbit.
card.wonder: If the Sun were a 1 cm marble, even this close neighbor would be about 700 km away.
card.connect: A short hop away in Eridanus, another neighbor has a companion that is already a dead star.
card.photoCaption: No ordinary photograph shows its planet or dust; radio and infrared telescopes revealed them.
card.deeper: Greaves et al. (1998) imaged a dust ring peaking about 60 au from the star at 850 µm, a young analogue of the Kuiper belt. Mawet et al. (2019) combined 30 years of radial velocities with deep Keck imaging: ε Eri b has about 0.78 (+0.38/−0.12) Jupiter masses and orbits at 3.48 au every 7.37 years. Gaia EDR3 gives 10.5 light-years.

teffK.note: carbon-star model atmosphere analysis

bv.note: non-simultaneous B and V; indicative only

superlatives.claim: one of the reddest stars in binocular reach
superlatives.scope: stars reaching binocular brightness at maximum

card.question: Why is Hind’s Crimson Star so deeply red?
card.answer: In air that cool the carbon forms molecules and soot that soak up blue light, so only the deepest red escapes, like sunlight seen through wildfire smoke.
card.glance: Near maximum, a small deep-red ember in Lepus; near minimum, too faint for binoculars.
card.whyHere: R Leporis is one of the reddest stars you can see, a glowing ember among white stars.
card.see: Drop south from Rigel into Lepus, the Hare, and look about 3½° west-north-west of μ Leporis. Near maximum it glows a startling deep red among white stars; judge it with short glances rather than a long stare. Near minimum you may not find it at all.
card.understand: R Leporis is an old giant in one of the last stages of a Sun-like star’s life. Roughly every 14 months it swells and shrinks, changing brightness by a factor of a few hundred. Deep inside it has fused helium into carbon, and convection, the same churning that stirs a pot of soup, has carried that carbon up to a surface of only about 2,400 K.
card.wonder: Some of the carbon in your body came from stars like this one, puffed into space and folded into new stars and planets.
card.connect: Betelgeuse is red too, but it is a far heavier star whose surface is rich in oxygen, not carbon.
card.photoCaption: Color photos show an intense red point; the hue is real, but cameras exaggerate how vivid it looks to the eye.
card.deeper: GCVS lists a Mira-type range of 5.5–11.7 V and a period of 427 days (VSX gives 437 days). Lambert et al. (1986) analyzed it among 30 cool carbon stars, with an effective temperature near 2,400 K. Gaia EDR3 places it about 1,500 light-years away. Its catalog color index (B−V ≈ 5.7) is not simultaneous and only indicative, but it is among the largest of any naked-eye or binocular star.

eventDependent.note: R Lep varies between about 5.5 and 11.7 over about 14 months and may be invisible in binoculars tonight. Check AAVSO for its current brightness.

radiusRsun.note: Rosseland angular diameter 11.3 ± 0.3 mas × maser distance

superlatives.claim: one of the largest stars known, and the largest within binocular reach
superlatives.scope: stars brighter than about 9th magnitude; radius estimates depend on method and distance

card.question: How big can a star get?
card.answer: About as big as VY Canis Majoris: some 1,400 times the Sun’s radius, so that in the Sun’s place its surface would reach beyond Jupiter’s orbit.
card.glance: A faint orange point in Canis Major, easy to pass over unless you know what it is.
card.whyHere: VY Canis Majoris is one of the largest stars known, and it sits within reach of your binoculars.
card.see: Start at τ Canis Majoris and its little cluster, south-east of Sirius, then move about 1¼° south-east to a dull orange point among white stars. It looks faint only because it is far away and wrapped in its own dust.
card.understand: VY Canis Majoris is a red supergiant, the bloated old age of a very heavy star. Measuring it took two clever steps. An interferometer measured how wide its disk looks, about a hundredth of an arcsecond, and radio astronomers timed the yearly shift of masers, natural microwave beacons in the gas around it, to get a distance of about 3,900 light-years; angle times distance gives the true size.
card.wonder: It is shedding gas so fast that Hubble images show it wrapped in a vast, tangled cocoon of dust, like smoke around a fire.
card.connect: Betelgeuse, the more familiar red supergiant, is about half its size and far closer.
card.photoCaption: Hubble images reveal arcs and knots of ejected dust around it; binoculars show only an orange point.
card.notSee: The dusty arcs and knots seen by Hubble.
card.deeper: Wittkowski et al. (2012) measured a photospheric angular diameter of 11.3 ± 0.3 mas with VLTI/AMBER; with the maser-parallax distance of 1.20 (+0.13/−0.10) kpc (Zhang et al. 2012) this gives 1,420 ± 120 solar radii and 3,490 ± 90 K, near the coolest limit for stars of 25–32 initial solar masses. Gaia’s parallax is unreliable for it because of its dusty, lopsided envelope.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness wanders between about 6.5 and 9.6; it can be a binocular challenge. Check AAVSO.

distanceLy.note: parallax 2.78 ± 0.18 mas; HST Fine Guidance Sensor parallax

teffK.note: median of 143 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2023A&A...678A.195D phase-resolved values 5,210–5,320 K; varies through the cycle)

historyHook.text: In 2000 an interferometer watched its disk swell and shrink as it pulsed, a direct measurement of a Cepheid breathing.

card.question: How can a star’s pulse tell you how far away it is?
card.answer: Time the rhythm and you know the star’s true power; compare that with how faint it looks and the distance follows, just as a lamp’s dimness tells you how far away it is once you know its wattage.
card.glance: A yellowish star in Gemini that brightens and fades on a 10-day rhythm.
card.whyHere: ζ Geminorum is a pulsating yardstick, one of the stars that let astronomers stretch distance measurements out to other galaxies.
card.see: Find ζ Geminorum about 7° north-east of Alhena, at the twins’ feet. Over a week or two, compare it with δ and λ Geminorum nearby: at its brightest it matches them, at its faintest it falls clearly behind.
card.understand: ζ Geminorum is a Cepheid, a yellow supergiant that rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every 10.15 days. In 2000 an interferometer actually watched its disk grow and shrink, a star breathing in plain view. Cepheids obey a remarkable rule, first noticed by Henrietta Leavitt: the slower the rhythm, the more light the star truly gives out, and the Hubble Space Telescope measured this star’s parallax to help calibrate that rule.
card.wonder: Stars of this kind, spotted in other galaxies, first showed that the universe extends far beyond the Milky Way.
card.connect: Its neighbor ε Geminorum is a similar yellow supergiant that does not pulse at all.
card.photoCaption: A photo freezes one moment of its 10-day cycle; it looks like any yellow star.
card.deeper: Benedict et al. (2007) measured its parallax with Hubble’s Fine Guidance Sensor, 2.78 ± 0.18 mas (about 1,170 light-years), as one of ten Cepheids anchoring the Galactic period–luminosity relation. Lane et al. (2000) detected its angular-diameter pulsation with the Palomar Testbed Interferometer. GCVS gives a period of 10.15 days and a range of 3.62–4.18 V.

multiplicity.systemNote: Six stars: A, B and C are each close binaries; A–B orbit in about 467 years (Torres & Ribas 2002).

card.question: How many stars are hiding in Castor?
card.answer: Six stars in three pairs, all bound by gravity, share the light you see as one white point.
card.glance: The fainter of Gemini’s twin stars: crisp white, beside orange Pollux.
card.whyHere: Castor looks like one crisp white star, and it turns out to be one of the best places to learn how stars are weighed.
card.see: Compare Castor’s white with Pollux’s orange, 4½° away. At 10× Castor looks single, because its two bright stars are only 5 arcseconds apart. With braced binoculars, look about 70 arcseconds south-south-east for a very faint point: Castor C.
card.understand: Castor A and Castor B circle each other over several centuries. Each is a tight pair of its own, revealed by the way the lines in its spectrum split and merge as the stars swing around. Castor C is two small red stars called red dwarfs that eclipse each other every 19½ hours, and timing those eclipses weighed each one to better than 1%.
card.wonder: Castor C’s two red dwarfs each weigh about 0.6 Suns, which makes the faintest pair in the family the best-measured.
card.connect: Its ‘twin’ Pollux is nothing like it: an orange giant with a planet.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split Castor A and B; binoculars show one white star and, at best, faint Castor C.
card.deeper: Torres & Ribas (2002) measured YY Gem (Castor C): two nearly identical M dwarfs of 0.599 solar masses and 0.62 solar radii in a 0.814-day orbit. Re-reducing the Hipparcos data while allowing for the 467-year A–B orbit, they found a parallax of 66.90 ± 0.63 mas (about 49 light-years) and estimated an age of roughly 370 million years. WDS lists A–B at 5.4″ and A–C at 70″ (2023).

teffK.note: median of 68 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2025A&A...703A.128B 4,868 K; 2024A&A...691A.160S 4,862 K)

superlatives.claim: one of the nearest giant stars to the Sun
superlatives.scope: giant stars (luminosity class III or brighter); Arcturus is next at about 37 light-years

card.question: Can a planet survive its star turning into a giant?
card.answer: This one has survived so far, a planet at least twice Jupiter’s mass still circling at about 1.6 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, well clear of its swollen star.
card.glance: The brighter of Gemini’s twins: a warm orange point.
card.whyHere: Pollux is one of the nearest giant stars to us, and it has kept a planet through the swelling of old age.
card.see: Put Pollux and Castor in one field: Pollux is orange, Castor white, and a touch of defocus makes the difference vivid. The ‘twins’ lie at different distances and are at different stages of life.
card.understand: Pollux is an orange giant about 34 light-years away that has finished burning hydrogen in its core, swollen, and cooled to about 4,850 K. Its planet gives itself away by tugging on the star. Pollux’s light shifts slightly toward blue, then toward red, every 590 days as the star swings toward and away from us, and astronomers followed that rhythm for 25 years before they were sure.
card.wonder: The same fate awaits the Sun, and whether Earth will survive it is a question astronomers still argue about.
card.connect: Procyon, to the south, is just about to begin this chapter of a star’s life.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point; the planet was found only by measuring the star’s tiny wobble.
card.deeper: Hatzes et al. (2006) confirmed with 25 years of radial velocities a 589.6-day, nearly circular orbit and a minimum mass of 2.3 Jupiter masses (for a 1.7-solar-mass star); Reffert et al. (2006) found 589.7 ± 3.5 days and 2.9 ± 0.3 Jupiter masses assuming 1.86 solar masses. The Hipparcos parallax, 96.54 ± 0.27 mas, gives 33.8 light-years.

card.question: How can you watch another star system’s orbit from your backyard?
card.answer: Catch λ Tauri in eclipse: for part of a night its light drops by about 40%, and you have watched one star slide in front of another hundreds of light-years away.
card.glance: A star in Taurus that dims every four days.
card.whyHere: λ Tauri is a star that winks, two stars eclipsing each other, so you can catch an orbit in the act with nothing but binoculars and patience.
card.see: λ Tauri lies about 5° west-south-west of γ Tauri, the point of the Hyades V. Normally it outshines γ Tauri, but during an eclipse it drops below it. Check it a few times on a night when the app predicts an eclipse and the change is plain.
card.understand: λ Tauri is an eclipsing binary: two stars orbiting so close, and seen so nearly edge-on, that the fainter passes in front of the brighter every 3.95 days. You cannot see either star’s disk, yet the shape of the dip tells you a great deal, because how long an eclipse lasts and how deep it goes depend on the sizes of the two stars and how fast they move. Timing dips like these is one of the main ways astronomers measure stars.
card.wonder: A third star circles the pair in a longer orbit, unseen, adding its own slow tug to the dance.
card.connect: Some eclipses last hours, but in Auriga one lasts nearly two years.
card.photoCaption: A photo shows a single bright star; the eclipses are only visible as changes over time.
card.deeper: GCVS classifies λ Tau as EA/DM with a period of 3.9529478 days and a V range of 3.37–3.91 (secondary minimum 3.54), with spectra B3 V and A4 IV, and a third star in a longer orbit. The Hipparcos 2007 parallax (6.74 ± 0.17 mas) puts the system about 480 light-years away; Gaia’s value for this bright binary is less certain.

card.question: How can a whole star hide behind another for weeks?
card.answer: The giant is so vast that the small star stays hidden behind it for weeks, and its light grazing the giant’s edge on the way in and out gives astronomers a free scan of a supergiant’s atmosphere.
card.glance: The western of the two lower Kids in Auriga, an orange-tinted star just south of Capella.
card.whyHere: ζ Aurigae pairs a cool supergiant with a small hot star, and every 2.7 years the giant swallows its companion from view.
card.see: From Capella, drop south to the Kids; the two lower Kids form a close pair, and ζ is the western one, orange-tinted beside whiter η Aurigae. The eclipse dims it by only about a fifth, so you need a careful comparison to notice.
card.understand: ζ Aurigae pairs an orange supergiant, a huge aging star, with a small hot blue-white one, and every 972 days the small star slips behind the big one. The best moments come just before and after, when the hot star shines through the giant’s thin outer atmosphere like a flashlight seen through fog. Reading that filtered light, astronomers can probe the layers of a star they cannot see as a disk.
card.wonder: The thin gas the hot star shines through is the giant’s own wind, slowly blowing out into space.
card.connect: Its neighbor ε Aurigae shows the reverse: a bright star hidden by a dark companion.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one orange-tinted star; both components blend into a single point.
card.deeper: GCVS: EA type, period 972.15 days, V 3.70–3.97, spectra K5 Ib–II plus B6.5 IV–V. The ‘atmospheric eclipse’ phases, when the B star shines through the supergiant’s outer layers, make ζ Aur a prototype for studying cool-supergiant winds. The Hipparcos 2007 parallax (4.15 ± 0.29 mas) gives about 790 light-years; Gaia EDR3’s value for this bright binary disagrees.

card.question: What does a star look like before it has fully switched on?
card.answer: Restless and uneven, glowing partly from its own contraction and from gas still raining onto it, and wrapped in the leftovers of the cloud that made it.
card.glance: A faint point near the limit of 50 mm binoculars, west of the Hyades, often out of reach.
card.whyHere: T Tauri is the original ‘baby star’, the model for young Sun-like stars that have not yet settled into adulthood, and our Sun once looked like this.
card.see: T Tauri lies about 1½° west of ε Tauri, the northern tip of the Hyades V. Under a dark sky, mounted 10×50s may show a faint star there, but its brightness changes and it may be out of reach tonight, so treat it as a challenge.
card.understand: T Tauri has not yet begun steady hydrogen burning in its core, and it shines partly by slowly shrinking, which heats its interior. Its light flickers as clumps of gas fall onto it from a surrounding disk and as dust drifts across our view. Radio astronomers followed a companion’s radio glow for two years and measured its yearly parallax shift, which puts the system about 481 light-years away.
card.wonder: That distance is known to within 0.4%, which makes T Tauri a ruler for the whole Taurus star-forming cloud.
card.connect: Nearby, the Pleiades show a batch of stars a hundred million years past this stage.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos show a small fan of nebula (Hind’s Variable Nebula) beside the star; binoculars do not.
card.notSee: Hind’s Variable Nebula (NGC 1555) and the infrared companions.
card.deeper: Loinard et al. (2007) tracked the radio-emitting companion T Tau Sb with the VLBA for two years and measured 147.6 ± 0.6 pc. GCVS lists a range of 9.3–13.5 V. T Tauri is a triple: the optically visible northern star and an infrared pair about 0.7″ to the south. It gave its name to the class of young, still-contracting Sun-like stars reviewed by Herbig (1977) and others.

eventDependent.note: Usually near 10th magnitude but has ranged 9.3–13.5; often invisible in binoculars.

card.question: What lights up the cloud around the Christmas Tree Cluster?
card.answer: The cloud is lit by 15 Monocerotis itself, whose ultraviolet light makes the leftover gas glow and slowly eats into the dark cloud that holds the Cone Nebula, the way spring sunshine wears down a snowbank.
card.glance: The bright ‘trunk’ star of the Christmas Tree Cluster in Monoceros.
card.whyHere: 15 Monocerotis stands at the base of the Christmas Tree Cluster, inside a cloud that is still glowing.
card.see: Sweep about 11° east of Betelgeuse to a small triangular group: the Christmas Tree Cluster, upside down, with 15 Mon as the bright star at its base. The Cone Nebula at the tree’s tip is for cameras only.
card.understand: 15 Monocerotis belongs to the hottest, heaviest class of stars, at the heart of the Christmas Tree Cluster, a family about five million years old. Gaia’s parallaxes for the cluster’s stars place the family about 2,300 light-years away, and models read its age from the colors and brightnesses of the members. Published temperatures for 15 Mon itself range widely, a reminder that a star wrapped in gas is hard to read.
card.wonder: It is so luminous that it still shows to the naked eye from that distance under dark skies.
card.connect: In Orion’s Sword, a similar heavy star still sits deep inside its glowing nebula.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo records faint nebulosity around the cluster that binoculars rarely show.
card.notSee: The Cone Nebula and the Fox Fur Nebula.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) put NGC 2264 at 700 pc with an age of about 5 (3.6–6.6) million years from Gaia DR3. 15 Mon is a 3″ visual binary (WDS) of an O7 V primary and a B1.5 V companion; published temperatures for the primary range from about 25,000 to 45,000 K depending on method. It is also cataloged as the slight variable S Mon.

card.question: How can one star outshine its whole cluster?
card.answer: By gathering the heaviest stars in one spot: τ CMa gives out so much light that it reaches naked-eye brightness from about 4,000 light-years, and its cluster mates are faint by comparison.
card.glance: A star sitting inside a tiny, sparkling cluster in Canis Major, south-east of Sirius.
card.whyHere: τ Canis Majoris is a knot of young, heavy stars so luminous that it outshines the entire cluster that bears its name.
card.see: Find τ Canis Majoris about 2½° north-east of Wezen, below and left of Sirius. In 10× binoculars a halo of faint stars surrounds it; at 7× the cluster may look like a soft glow around one bright star.
card.understand: τ CMa is a small group of very hot, very heavy stars, including a pair that eclipses every 1.3 days. Its cluster is only about five to seven million years old, an age astronomers read from its members: the faint ones are still settling down, while none of the heavy ones has yet burned out. Heavy stars are not just a little brighter than light ones but enormously so, which is why a handful can outshine all the rest.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 4,000 years ago, when the first written laws were being carved in Mesopotamia.
card.connect: Close by lies VY CMa, what a star this heavy becomes after a few million more years.
card.photoCaption: Photos resolve dozens of faint cluster stars around τ CMa; binoculars show a handful.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) give 1,228 pc and about 7 (4.3–9.3) million years for NGC 2362 from Gaia DR3; Moitinho et al. (2001) found 5 (+1/−2) million years at 1,480 pc from photometry and called the cluster a template for early stellar evolution. GCVS lists τ CMa as a 1.282-day eclipsing system of small amplitude.

card.question: Why do the Pleiades sisters all shine the same blue-white?
card.answer: They were born together from one cloud about 125 million years ago, and the brightest are all hot young stars, so the family resemblance is written in their color.
card.glance: A blue-white star on the western side of the Pleiades.
card.whyHere: Electra is one of the named sisters of the Pleiades, and her color is the family resemblance that gives the cluster away.
card.see: Center the Pleiades in Taurus, north-west of Aldebaran. Electra sits at the western end of the bowl, with Merope just south-east of it.
card.understand: All the Pleiades formed together from a single cloud, so they share an age and a distance. Among stars of the same age, color follows mass: the heavier the star, the hotter its surface and the bluer its light. The brightest sisters are all heavy stars with surfaces far hotter than the Sun’s.
card.wonder: In one old story Electra is the ‘lost Pleiad’, the sister who hid her face in grief at the fall of Troy.
card.connect: All these siblings share one birthday; a family five times older sits nearby in the Hyades.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures surround the bright Pleiades with blue dust; binoculars show clean points.

card.question: How do astronomers know Taygeta belongs to the Pleiades family?
card.answer: She moves with the family: same distance, same motion through space and the same 125-million-year age, a sibling by every test astronomers can apply.
card.glance: A blue-white star at the north-west corner of the Pleiades dipper.
card.whyHere: Taygeta is one of the named sisters of the Pleiades, and proving she belongs takes more than standing close by.
card.see: Center the Pleiades in Taurus, north-west of Aldebaran. Taygeta marks the north-western corner of the dipper, just north of Electra.
card.understand: Stars that merely line up on the sky can lie at very different distances, so membership needs real evidence. Gaia measured the parallaxes and motions of the Pleiades, and Taygeta sits at the cluster’s distance, about 440 light-years, and drifts across the sky in step with her sisters, like birds flying in formation. Her surface, about 14,000 K, fits the family too.
card.wonder: The flock will not last forever, because over hundreds of millions of years the galaxy’s tides will scatter these sisters across the sky.
card.connect: All these siblings share one birthday; a family five times older sits nearby in the Hyades.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures surround the bright Pleiades with blue dust; binoculars show clean points.

card.question: How hot is a young Pleiades star like Maia?
card.answer: About 14,000 K at the surface, more than twice as hot as the Sun, which is why Maia and her 125-million-year-old sisters glow blue-white.
card.glance: A blue-white star on the northern edge of the Pleiades bowl.
card.whyHere: Maia is one of the named sisters of the Pleiades, and her blue-white glow is a thermometer you can read by eye.
card.see: Center the Pleiades in Taurus, north-west of Aldebaran. Maia lies on the northern edge of the bowl, between Taygeta and Alcyone, and its blue-white matches the other bright members.
card.understand: A star’s color tells its temperature the way an electric stove ring does: dull red when warm, then orange, yellow-white and finally bluish as it gets hotter. Astronomers make that precise by measuring how a star’s light is shared across the rainbow. For Maia the balance tips strongly toward blue.
card.wonder: Maia once lent its name to a whole supposed class of pulsating stars, which later and better measurements could not confirm.
card.connect: All these siblings share one birthday; a family five times older sits nearby in the Hyades.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures surround the bright Pleiades with blue dust; binoculars show clean points.

card.question: Is Atlas a lone bright star or part of a family?
card.answer: Atlas is a Pleiad through and through, born from the same cloud as the sisters about 125 million years ago.
card.glance: The bright star at the east end of the Pleiades, with faint Pleione beside it.
card.whyHere: Atlas, the father of the Pleiades in myth, really does sit among the sisters, and here the old story got the family right.
card.see: Center the Pleiades in Taurus, north-west of Aldebaran. Atlas is the bright star at the eastern end of the handle, with fainter Pleione just north of it.
card.understand: Atlas is a hot star with a surface about 13,000 K, more than twice as hot as the Sun’s. It shares the cluster’s distance and its motion through space, the two tests that separate true members from stars that merely line up. Its color and brightness fit the same age as the others, too.
card.wonder: In the myth Atlas and Pleione are the parents, and here they sit side by side at the edge of their family.
card.connect: All these siblings share one birthday; a family five times older sits nearby in the Hyades.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures surround the bright Pleiades with blue dust; binoculars show clean points.

card.question: Where does the blue haze around the Pleiades come from?
card.answer: From an unrelated dust cloud the Pleiades happen to be drifting through, lit by the cluster as it passes.
card.glance: A blue-white star at the south-west corner of the Pleiades bowl.
card.whyHere: Merope is wrapped in the brightest patch of the famous blue haze that every photograph of the Pleiades shows.
card.see: Merope is the south-western corner of the Pleiades bowl. Under a very dark sky, glance slightly to one side and look for a faint smudge just south of it; most nights you will see only the star.
card.understand: The haze is starlight reflected off dust, blue for the same reason the daytime sky is: small particles scatter blue light more than red. People long assumed it was the cluster’s birth cloud. But the gas and the stars move at different speeds and in different directions, which a family and its nest would not.
card.wonder: The cloud and the cluster are going different ways, and in time they will part.
card.connect: The Hyades, a family five times older, have no haze at all.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the Merope Nebula as a bright blue fan; binoculars show it rarely, if ever.
card.deeper: The reflection nebula NGC 1435 around Merope is dust the cluster is passing through, shown by the different motions of the gas and the stars (NOIRLab release noao0315, after Gibson & Nordsieck 2003).

card.question: Why has one Hyades star already turned into a giant?
card.answer: It was born slightly heavier, so it reached old age first while its lighter siblings are still in their long adult lives.
card.glance: A yellow-orange star at the point of the Hyades V, where its two arms meet.
card.whyHere: γ Tauri, at the point of the V, is one of four Hyades stars that have already aged into giants.
card.see: In the Hyades, the V-shaped face of Taurus, find the star at the point where the two arms meet. Its yellow-orange tint is paler than Aldebaran’s.
card.understand: Its siblings, born with it about 625 million years ago, are still white or yellowish. This one began a little heavier, and a heavier star burns its core hydrogen disproportionately fast, the way a car with a bigger engine empties its tank sooner despite carrying more fuel. Having run out, it swelled into a giant and now burns helium instead.
card.wonder: Four giants in one cluster, all at the same stage, are a crowd-sourced clue to the cluster’s age.
card.connect: Its giant siblings share the V, and one of them has a planet.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the same yellowish point; the color is subtle but real.

card.question: What can four giants in one cluster tell you?
card.answer: They mark the line between stars that have aged and stars that have not, and that line dates the Hyades to about 625 million years.
card.glance: A yellow-orange star partway up the northern arm of the Hyades V, with δ² and δ³ nearby.
card.whyHere: δ¹ Tauri is another of the Hyades’ four giants, and together they work like a clock hand pointing at the cluster’s age.
card.see: In the Hyades, the V-shaped face of Taurus, follow the northern arm partway up to δ¹, with δ² and δ³ close by. Its yellow-orange tint is paler than Aldebaran’s.
card.understand: All four giants share the same color and brightness, so they are at the same stage of life. Since the Hyades were born together, these are the heaviest stars to have reached that stage so far. Models say how long a star of their mass takes to get there, and that is the cluster’s age.
card.wonder: The Hyades are about five times older than the Pleiades, and it shows: the younger cluster has no giants at all.
card.connect: Its giant siblings share the V, and one of them has a planet.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the same yellowish point; the color is subtle but real.

teffK.note: median of 63 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2024A&A...692A.189R 4,939 K)

superlatives.claim: first planet found around a star in an open cluster

card.question: How can we know the age of a planet’s star?
card.answer: Find the star a family: as a Hyades member, Ain and its planet share the cluster’s age of about 625 million years.
card.glance: A yellow-orange star at the northern tip of the Hyades V.
card.whyHere: Ain is the first star in an open cluster found to have a planet, and its cluster lends that planet something rare: a known birthday.
card.see: Ain is ε Tauri, the star at the tip of the northern arm of the Hyades V. Aldebaran, at the other tip, is brighter and more orange.
card.understand: Ain is a giant in the Hyades, an open cluster: a loose family of stars born together from one cloud. A regular 595-day wobble in its speed revealed a planet at least seven times Jupiter’s mass. A lone star’s age is hard to measure, but a cluster’s can be read from the whole family at once.
card.wonder: Its planet orbits about twice as far from its star as Earth does from the Sun.
card.connect: The Twins in Gemini hold another giant with a planet: Pollux.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one yellowish point; the planet was found from the star’s wobble.
card.deeper: Sato et al. (2007) found a 594.9-day orbit with a minimum mass of 7.6 Jupiter masses at 1.93 au, adopting 2.7 solar masses from isochrones. Arentoft et al. (2019) used its oscillations (asteroseismology) to test its mass and stage. Gaia EDR3 puts it at 146 light-years.

teffK.note: median of 4 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2016A&A...585A...7K 8,091 K)

card.question: Are two stars that look like a pair really together?
card.answer: Only some of them are. Others just happen to line up by chance, and binoculars alone can never tell you which kind of pair you are looking at.
card.glance: A wide, easy pair of white stars north of the Hyades.
card.whyHere: κ Tauri is an easy binocular double among the outlying Hyades stars, the kind of pair that makes you wonder whether the two know each other.
card.see: Look about 6° north of the Hyades V, the face of Taurus. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 5.7 arcminutes apart (an arcminute is a sixtieth of a degree).
card.understand: Both stars are white and hotter than the Sun. A pair on the sky may be true companions or a near star and a far one that happen to line up. The tests are distance and motion: real partners share both, while a chance pair gives itself away once their parallaxes are measured.
card.wonder: Under a dark sky, keen eyes can split this pair without any optics.
card.connect: Back in the V, Aldebaran is the clearest impostor of all.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the two white stars much as binoculars do.

teffK.note: median of 6 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2024A&A...683A.125P 8,024 K)

card.question: Is a pair of stars side by side always a real couple?
card.answer: Side by side on the sky can still mean far apart in depth, and the bright orange neighbor is the proof.
card.glance: A wide, easy pair of white stars about 1° south-east of Aldebaran.
card.whyHere: σ Tauri is a wide white pair beside Aldebaran, and the bright orange star next to it shows how easily the sky can fool you.
card.see: Look about 1° south-east of Aldebaran in Taurus. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 7.4 arcminutes apart (an arcminute is a sixtieth of a degree), nearly equal in brightness.
card.understand: Both stars are white and hotter than the Sun, and the brighter lies about 179 light-years away. Whether the other star sits at the same depth is the whole question, since lining up on the sky costs nothing. Only measured distances and motions tell a real couple from two strangers.
card.wonder: A degree from Aldebaran and nearly three times as far away, it shares a binocular field with the sky’s best-known impostor.
card.connect: Back in the V, Aldebaran is the clearest impostor of all.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the two white stars much as binoculars do.

card.question: Are Orion’s two shoulders neighbors in space?
card.answer: Bellatrix lies about 250 light-years away, roughly half as far as Betelgeuse, and only from Earth do the two line up into the shoulders of one hunter.
card.glance: Orion’s western shoulder, a blue-white star opposite orange Betelgeuse.
card.whyHere: Bellatrix, Orion’s other shoulder, seems to balance Betelgeuse across the hunter’s chest.
card.see: Put Bellatrix in the field, then swing across to Betelgeuse: blue-white against orange. They look similar in brightness, yet they are very different stars at very different distances.
card.understand: Bellatrix is a hot blue-white star whose yearly parallax shift, measured by the Hipparcos satellite, puts it much closer than the Belt stars. A constellation is a pattern drawn on a flat sky. The stars that make it can lie at wildly different depths, like streetlights on different streets lining up when seen from one window.
card.wonder: Seen from another star system, Orion’s outline would fall apart.
card.connect: Between the two shoulders runs a thermometer: blue-white is hot, orange is cool.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: How far away is Mintaka, really?
card.answer: About 1,380 light-years, roughly twice the satellite figure, which places Mintaka among its Orion siblings near the σ Orionis cluster.
card.glance: The right-hand star of Orion’s Belt, with a much fainter companion to its north that steady 10× binoculars split.
card.whyHere: Mintaka, the western Belt star, is a family of heavy stars whose distance has been surprisingly hard to pin down.
card.see: Center Mintaka, the Belt star nearest Rigel’s side. Look about 52 arcseconds due north for a much fainter companion; steady 10× binoculars split it.
card.understand: Mintaka is a group of hot, heavy stars whose inner pair eclipses every 5.7 days, dimming it slightly. Satellite measurements of its parallax, the tiny yearly shift that gives distance, put it surprisingly close. But at that distance its stars came out too faint for their temperatures and masses, so astronomers turned the logic around and asked what distance makes everything consistent.
card.wonder: Mintaka sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises due east and sets due west from anywhere on Earth.
card.connect: Its Belt neighbors belong to the same young family.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the bright star and its companion; the eclipses only show over time.

card.question: How can the hotter of Orion’s two feet look fainter?
card.answer: Much of Saiph’s light is ultraviolet, invisible to us, so it looks fainter than Rigel even though it is closer and hotter.
card.glance: Orion’s lower-left foot, a blue-white star a bit fainter than Rigel.
card.whyHere: Saiph is hotter than Rigel yet looks fainter, a lesson in how much of a star’s light our eyes simply miss.
card.see: Compare Saiph with Rigel at Orion’s opposite foot. Rigel looks brighter, both are blue-white, and nothing hints that Saiph is the hotter star.
card.understand: Saiph’s surface is more than twice as hot as Rigel’s. Heat a body and its glow shifts toward shorter wavelengths, the way a poker goes from red to yellow to white; a star this hot pours much of its energy out as invisible ultraviolet. Saiph is even the closer of the two, so distance is no excuse.
card.wonder: Our eyes evolved under sunlight, and they miss most of what a star this hot gives out.
card.connect: Above Saiph, Orion’s Belt holds three more hot stars from Orion’s young family.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: What flung two stars right out of Orion?
card.answer: Most likely ι Orionis itself, in a close brush with another pair that sent the two runaways off in opposite directions.
card.glance: The bright star at the bottom of Orion’s Sword, just south of the Orion Nebula.
card.whyHere: ι Orionis, at the tip of Orion’s Sword, is a tight pair of stars with a violent past.
card.see: The Sword ends in ι Orionis, just below the Orion Nebula. Binoculars show a scatter of fainter stars around it, the young cluster NGC 1980.
card.understand: ι Orionis is a close pair of heavy stars on a stretched orbit, an odd shape for so tight a pair and a hint of a violent past. Traced backward, the runaways AE Aurigae and μ Columbae both lead here, to about 2.5 million years ago. When two pairs of stars pass that close, gravity can swap partners and fling two of them away at high speed.
card.wonder: Two stars now on opposite sides of the sky were once neighbors here.
card.connect: One of the runaways, AE Aurigae, now sits far to the north in Auriga.
card.photoCaption: Wide photos show the Orion Nebula’s outer glow reaching toward ι Ori.

historyHook.text: Its tight, eccentric pair is the likely culprit that ejected AE Aurigae and μ Columbae about 2.5 million years ago.

card.question: Is the Trapezium the only hot star lighting the Orion Nebula?
card.answer: It has help from θ² Orionis A, born alongside the Trapezium, which lights the nebula’s southern edge, though the Trapezium remains the main power plant.
card.glance: A pair of points just south-east of the Orion Nebula’s bright core.
card.whyHere: θ² Orionis is a second young, hot system inside the Orion Nebula, and binoculars can split it.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula’s bright core in Orion’s Sword and look just south-east. θ² Orionis A and B, about 52 arcseconds apart, split with steady 10×50s at the edge of the brightest glow.
card.understand: θ² Orionis A is a hot young star born with the Trapezium about a million years ago. Its ultraviolet light strips electrons from hydrogen at the nebula’s southern edge, and the gas glows as the electrons are recaptured. Like the Trapezium stars, it formed inside the very cloud it is now lighting up.
card.wonder: These stars began to shine when our ancestors were already walking upright.
card.connect: The real powerhouse is the Trapezium just to the north-west.
card.photoCaption: Photos bury θ² in the nebula’s glow; binoculars show it as a crisp pair.
