card.question: What happens when a star spins almost fast enough to fly apart?
card.answer: It sheds a disk of gas from its equator, and ζ Tauri’s light dims and changes as that disk grows and fades.
card.glance: The tip of Taurus’s southern horn, a blue-white star.
card.whyHere: ζ Tauri is a fast-spinning star wrapped in its own gas disk, and it doubles as the signpost to the Crab Nebula.
card.see: From Aldebaran, follow the Bull’s southern horn out to its tip: that is ζ Tauri. The Crab Nebula lies about 1° to the north-west, a faint smudge for dark skies only.
card.understand: ζ Tauri spins so fast that gas leaks from its equator into a flat disk. We see that disk nearly edge-on, so it absorbs some starlight on the way to us, leaving dark ‘shell’ lines in the spectrum. A companion star circles it every 133 days.
card.wonder: A disk like this can spread much wider than the star itself.
card.connect: Just beside it lies the Crab Nebula, the wreck of an exploded star.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point; the disk is far too small to image.

card.question: Can a young star suddenly grow hundreds of times brighter?
card.answer: FU Orionis did exactly that, and young stars may build themselves up in bursts just like this one.
card.glance: A faint point near the limit of 50 mm binoculars, north of Betelgeuse, and a challenge.
card.whyHere: FU Orionis flared up and never came back down, and it named a whole class of stellar growth spurts.
card.see: FU Orionis lies about 2½° east-south-east of Meissa, the little triangle at Orion’s head above Betelgeuse. Under dark skies, mounted binoculars may just show a faint star there.
card.understand: In the late 1930s FU Orionis brightened several-hundred-fold and has stayed bright ever since. Its spectrum gave the game away: it looks like a supergiant’s, yet the star is young and small. The light comes from a hot disk of gas around it, which suddenly began pouring material onto the star and heated up until it outshone the star itself.
card.wonder: Its outburst has lasted for decades, one ‘flare’ longer than most human lifetimes.
card.connect: T Tauri, in Taurus, is the model for steadier young stars.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a faint star with a small fan of nebulosity.

historyHook.text: In the late 1930s it brightened several-hundred-fold and has stayed bright ever since.

eventDependent.note: Still in its long outburst near 9–10th magnitude; check AAVSO.

card.question: Why does W Orionis glow so warmly red?
card.answer: Carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere filter out the blue and leave a warm red glow, like a lamp seen through smoked glass.
card.glance: An orange-red star in western Orion, easy in binoculars.
card.whyHere: W Orionis is one of the warmest-colored stars in Orion, an aging giant with an unusual recipe.
card.see: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion’s western shoulder. Among white field stars it stands out as orange-red, and a slight defocus boosts the color.
card.understand: W Orionis is an old giant that fuses helium into carbon in a shell deep inside, and every so often its churning outer layers reach down and dredge some of that carbon up to the surface. In its cool atmosphere, about 2,700 K, the carbon forms molecules that soak up blue light. It also varies slowly in brightness, over about seven months.
card.wonder: Stars like this are a major source of the carbon in the galaxy, including the carbon in you.
card.connect: An even redder carbon star waits in Lepus, below Orion.
card.photoCaption: Color photos exaggerate its red; the eye sees orange-red.

eventDependent.note: Varies between about 5.5 and 6.9; check AAVSO for its current brightness.

card.question: What gives Zaurak its orange color?
card.answer: Zaurak’s swollen surface runs well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, and a glow that cool comes out orange, never white.
card.glance: The brightest star in this part of Eridanus, with a clear orange tint.
card.whyHere: Zaurak is a cool red giant on the first big bend of Eridanus, the River, and its color is a temperature you can read by eye.
card.see: Follow Eridanus west of Rigel; Zaurak is the brightest star on the River’s first big bend. Compare its orange with white Cursa near Rigel.
card.understand: Zaurak is a red giant, an aging star that has swollen and cooled, about 190 light-years away. Every hot object glows, and the color of the glow follows its temperature, red when cooler and bluish when hotter. Zaurak’s surface sits around 3,800 K, cool by stellar standards, so most of its visible light is orange and red.
card.wonder: The light you see left Zaurak in the 1830s, just as astronomers were first measuring the distance to a star.
card.connect: Nearby in Eridanus are two neighbor stars far closer to us.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point.

card.question: Is Cursa as far away as its neighbor Rigel?
card.answer: Cursa is a near neighbor and Rigel a distant giant, which outshines it only because it is so much more powerful.
card.glance: A white star just north-west of Rigel, at the head of Eridanus.
card.whyHere: Cursa sits at Rigel’s feet like a footstool, and the two make one of the sky’s best lessons in judging distance.
card.see: Find Rigel and look about 3° north-west for a white star: Cursa. Both look white-blue, and Rigel is much brighter.
card.understand: Cursa is a white star about 90 light-years away, a distance Gaia measured from its yearly parallax shift with an error of about one percent. Rigel, by the same method, is nearly ten times farther. Yet Rigel still looks brighter, and a lamp that outshines a nearer one from ten times farther away must be vastly more powerful.
card.wonder: Move Rigel to Cursa’s distance and it would outshine every star in the sky.
card.connect: Farther along the River, Zaurak’s orange shows a much cooler kind of star.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: Why does nearby Nihal look fainter than distant Arneb?
card.answer: Arneb is a supergiant that gives out so much more light that it outshines Nihal across a far greater distance.
card.glance: A yellowish star in Lepus, just south-west of Arneb, below Orion’s feet.
card.whyHere: Nihal is a yellow giant much nearer than its neighbor Arneb, yet Arneb looks brighter, and the pair makes a quick lesson in true power.
card.see: Put Nihal and Arneb, the two brightest stars of Lepus below Orion, in the same field. Arneb is slightly brighter and whiter, Nihal yellowish.
card.understand: Nihal is a yellow giant about 160 light-years away, measured by Gaia’s parallax. Arneb, beside it, is more than ten times farther. Ten times the distance spreads a star’s light over a hundred times the area, so to look brighter from there, Arneb must give out more than a hundred times as much light.
card.wonder: Nihal’s light left in the 1870s; Arneb’s left around 200 BCE, in the days of the Roman Republic.
card.connect: Arneb, right beside it, is the distant powerhouse.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellowish point.

card.question: How bright is Arneb, really?
card.answer: Tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun, a power that distance shrinks to a moderately bright star in a faint constellation.
card.glance: The brightest star of Lepus, below Orion’s feet, white with a hint of cream.
card.whyHere: Arneb is a distant supergiant, and it looks modest only because its light has come so far.
card.see: Find Lepus, the Hare, below Rigel and Saiph. Arneb is its brightest star; compare it with nearby Nihal, which is far closer but looks fainter.
card.understand: Arneb is a supergiant, one of the most luminous kinds of star, about 2,200 light-years away. Working out its power takes two measurements: how bright it looks, and how far away it is. The second is the hard part, because its parallax is tiny, and since power scales with the distance squared, a modest error in distance becomes a large one in power.
card.wonder: Its light left over 2,000 years ago, in the days of the Roman Republic.
card.connect: Lepus also hides one of the reddest stars in the sky.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: Why is one corner of Auriga orange?
card.answer: ι Aurigae is simply cooler than the stars around it, an aging giant whose surface runs well below Capella’s, so it glows a warmer color.
card.glance: The orange star at Auriga’s south-western corner.
card.whyHere: ι Aurigae is an orange giant that gives the Auriga pentagon its one warm corner.
card.see: Look at the pentagon of Auriga, with Capella at its top. Its south-western corner is ι Aurigae, distinctly orange next to yellowish Capella and white Menkalinan.
card.understand: ι Aurigae is a luminous orange giant about 450 light-years away. Its surface is near 4,200 K, cooler than Capella’s stars, so its light leans toward the red. It is a star well into old age, swollen and cooled after the hydrogen in its core ran out.
card.wonder: From its distance our Sun would be a faint speck that needs a telescope to see.
card.connect: East along the Milky Way, Auriga’s star clusters wait.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point.

card.question: How can two stars eclipse each other without anyone noticing?
card.answer: When they are near-twins seen almost edge-on: Menkalinan’s two white stars do eclipse each other, but each eclipse dims it by less than a tenth, too little for the eye.
card.glance: The second-brightest star of Auriga, white, at the pentagon’s eastern corner.
card.whyHere: Menkalinan is a pair of nearly identical stars that eclipse each other every four days.
card.see: Find the Auriga pentagon, with Capella at its top; Menkalinan is the white star at its eastern corner. Its eclipses are invisible to the eye, so enjoy it as a steady beacon.
card.understand: Menkalinan is a pair of twin white stars orbiting every 3.96 days. Seen almost edge-on, they take turns eclipsing each other. Because they are twins, each eclipse looks much like the other, and the small dips together with the stars’ measured speeds let astronomers weigh and measure both.
card.wonder: Two whole stars orbit each other in under four days, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
card.connect: Auriga holds a far more dramatic eclipse at the Kids.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one white point.

card.question: How can a star’s light wobble as it spins?
card.answer: Its patches swing into and out of view as it rotates, like a lighthouse with a smudged lens, changing its brightness very slightly.
card.glance: A white star on the south-eastern side of the Auriga pentagon.
card.whyHere: θ Aurigae is a white star in the Auriga pentagon whose light rises and falls on a beat of a few days.
card.see: On the Auriga pentagon, θ Aurigae is the white star between Menkalinan and Elnath. Its close companion needs a telescope.
card.understand: θ Aurigae has strong magnetic fields that gather certain elements, such as silicon, into patches on its surface. Those patches absorb and re-emit light differently from the rest of the surface, so the star looks a little brighter from one side than from the other. Measuring how its brightness and spectrum repeat tells astronomers that it turns every 3.6 days.
card.wonder: These patches can last for decades, a kind of weather that never changes.
card.connect: At Taurus’s horn, a fast-spinning star wears a disk of its own gas.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one white point.

card.question: Can one star belong to two constellations?
card.answer: Elnath served both Taurus and Auriga for centuries, but under today’s official boundaries it belongs to Taurus alone.
card.glance: A blue-white star where the Bull’s northern horn meets Auriga’s pentagon.
card.whyHere: Elnath sits exactly where two star patterns meet, the Bull’s northern horn and the Charioteer’s pentagon.
card.see: Elnath completes the Auriga pentagon and also marks the tip of Taurus’s northern horn. Compare its blue-white with orange ι Aurigae across the pentagon.
card.understand: Elnath is a hot blue-white star about 130 light-years away. For centuries star charts drew it into both the Bull and the Charioteer. When astronomers agreed on official boundaries about a century ago, every point of the sky went to exactly one constellation, and Elnath went to Taurus.
card.wonder: The light you see left Elnath in the 1890s, a generation before astronomers settled that it belongs to Taurus and not to Auriga.
card.connect: The southern horn tip points toward the Crab Nebula.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Can we watch a planet being born?
card.answer: Around AB Aurigae we seem to be watching just that, a giant planet gathering itself out of the disk.
card.glance: A star in Auriga, easy in binoculars but unremarkable to look at.
card.whyHere: AB Aurigae is a young star in Auriga, still young enough to be wrapped in the leftovers of its birth.
card.see: AB Aurigae lies about 2½° south of ι Aurigae, the orange star at Auriga’s south-western corner. It looks like any faint field star, and the drama is in what telescopes found around it.
card.understand: The star is still surrounded by its birth disk of gas and dust. Images from Hubble and the Subaru Telescope show spiral arms in the disk and, about three times Neptune’s distance from the star, a bright clump. Spiral arms are what a growing planet should stir up, and the clump sits right where those arms say a planet should be.
card.wonder: You are looking at a planetary system in its infancy, roughly 500 light-years away.
card.connect: T Tauri in Taurus shows a star younger still, wrapped in its cloud.
card.photoCaption: Telescope images show its spiral disk; binoculars show only the star.
card.deeper: Currie et al. (2022) used Subaru and Hubble to find evidence of a Jovian protoplanet at a projected separation of about 93 au, embedded in the disk and probably responsible for its spiral features. Gaia EDR3 puts the star about 510 light-years away.

eventDependent.note: Dust in its disk can dim it unpredictably between about 6.9 and 8.9.

card.question: Where does the carbon in your body come from?
card.answer: Partly from stars like UU Aurigae, which make carbon, bring it to the surface and puff it into space, where it ends up in new stars, planets and eventually people.
card.glance: An orange-red star in eastern Auriga.
card.whyHere: UU Aurigae is an old red giant in eastern Auriga, and its color is a chemical signature.
card.see: Look in eastern Auriga, between Capella and the Gemini twins: among white stars, one glows orange-red. Judge its color with short glances rather than a stare.
card.understand: UU Aurigae has fused helium into carbon deep inside, and its churning outer layers have dredged that carbon up to the surface. Carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere, about 2,800 K, absorb blue light and leave a warm red glow. A slow wind carries its outer layers, carbon dust and all, out into space.
card.wonder: Every atom of carbon in you has been through a star at least once.
card.connect: W Orionis, across the sky in Orion, is another carbon star to compare.
card.photoCaption: Color photos make it look redder than the eye sees.

eventDependent.note: Varies between about 5.1 and 6.6; check AAVSO.

card.question: What kind of star stands at Gemini’s feet?
card.answer: A white star hotter and heavier than the Sun, just beginning the change that will turn it into a giant.
card.glance: The bright white star at the feet of Gemini.
card.whyHere: Alhena is a white signpost star at Gemini’s feet, a near neighbor in stellar terms.
card.see: Follow the Gemini twins down from Castor and Pollux to their feet; Alhena is the brightest star there. Use it as a jumping-off point for ζ Geminorum to the north-east.
card.understand: Alhena is a white star with a surface about 9,300 K, roughly one and a half times as hot as the Sun’s, about 110 light-years away. Its spectrum shows it has started to leave the long, steady phase of burning hydrogen in its core, the same change Procyon is going through. Before long, by stellar standards, it will swell into a giant.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time of the First World War.
card.connect: North-east of Alhena, ζ Geminorum pulses like a slow heartbeat.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

teffK.note: median of 22 published values in SIMBAD (e.g. 2014AJ....147..137L 4,525 K)

card.question: Why does Mebsuta shine steadily when its cousin ζ Geminorum pulses?
card.answer: Mebsuta is too cool to sit inside that narrow band, so its valve never catches and the star shines steadily.
card.glance: A yellow-orange star on Castor’s side of Gemini.
card.whyHere: Mebsuta is a yellow supergiant much like ζ Geminorum, yet it shines steadily.
card.see: Follow Castor’s ‘body’ down Gemini; Mebsuta is the yellow-orange star halfway. Compare its color with ζ Geminorum to the south-east.
card.understand: Mebsuta is a supergiant, one of the most luminous kinds of star, about 870 light-years away and cooler and redder than ζ Geminorum. Cepheids, the stars that rhythmically swell and shrink, pulse only within a narrow range of surface temperatures. In that range a layer of helium inside the star acts like a valve, trapping heat as it is squeezed and releasing it as it expands, which keeps the pulsing going.
card.wonder: Far more luminous than the Sun, it still looks like an ordinary star from 870 light-years away.
card.connect: ζ Geminorum, to the south-east, is the pulsing kind.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellow-orange point.

card.question: Is every orange-red star a supergiant like Betelgeuse?
card.answer: Tejat matches Betelgeuse in color but is an ordinary red giant, far less luminous, so the same color can belong to very different stars.
card.glance: A clearly orange-red star at Castor’s foot, near the cluster M35.
card.whyHere: μ Geminorum is a cool red giant right beside the cluster M35, a color contrast you can take in with one sweep.
card.see: Find Gemini’s western foot. μ Geminorum is the orange-red star there, and the cluster M35 sits about 2° to its north-west.
card.understand: μ Geminorum is a red giant, an aging star swollen and cooled, about 230 light-years away. Its surface is near 3,600 K, the same as Betelgeuse’s, so the two share a color. But color tells you only temperature; true power needs distance too, and Tejat is less than half as far as Betelgeuse yet looks much fainter.
card.wonder: It also flickers slightly and irregularly in brightness, as many cool giants do.
card.connect: Next door, M35 holds a whole family of stars.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange-red point.

card.question: How many stars hide in one point of light at Gemini’s feet?
card.answer: There are at least two, and the true partner is the one star your binoculars will never show.
card.glance: A blue-white star at Gemini’s feet with a faint star beside it.
card.whyHere: ν Geminorum looks like an easy binocular double, but the split misleads, and a spinning star sits at its heart.
card.see: Find ν Geminorum at Gemini’s feet, near Alhena, and look about 2 arcminutes to the north-north-west for a much fainter star. Binoculars split it easily.
card.understand: ν Geminorum is a hot, fast-spinning star with a thin disk of gas around its equator. It is also a close pair that no telescope can split; the second star shows itself only in the spectrum, where the lines shift back and forth as the two orbit. The faint star beside it is no companion, just a nearer star on its own path.
card.wonder: Many bright stars that look single turn out to be crowded systems once someone takes a spectrum.
card.connect: The cluster M35 lies in the same sweep, to the north-west.

card.see: At binocular power Castor B merges with Castor A into one white point. A small telescope at 50× or more splits it.

card.question: How can a star sixty times farther than Sirius still be easy to see?
card.answer: Mirzam is a hot, powerful star that gives out far more light than Sirius, more than enough to shine brightly from that distance.
card.glance: A blue-white star just west of Sirius, ‘the announcer’ that rises first.
card.whyHere: Mirzam is the hot star that heralds Sirius, and it is far more powerful than its modest looks suggest.
card.see: Look about 5° west of Sirius for a blue-white star: Mirzam. Compare the two and Sirius looks dazzling, Mirzam modest.
card.understand: Mirzam is about 490 light-years away, nearly sixty times farther than Sirius. A star that far would need thousands of times Sirius’s output to match it, and Mirzam, though fainter, gets a respectable fraction of the way. It is a hot star that also pulses every six hours, far too slightly for the eye to notice.
card.wonder: Its name means ‘the announcer’, because it rises shortly before Sirius.
card.connect: Sirius, beside it, is bright because it is close, not because it is powerful.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Which is really the more powerful star, Sirius or Adhara?
card.answer: Adhara, which must outshine Sirius more than a hundred times over to look this bright from nearly fifty times the distance.
card.glance: A bright blue-white star in the hindquarters of Canis Major.
card.whyHere: Adhara is only the second-brightest star in Canis Major, which makes it easy to overlook beside Sirius.
card.see: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius’s white.
card.understand: Adhara is about 400 light-years away, nearly fifty times farther than Sirius, yet it is one of the brightest stars in the sky. Fifty times the distance means some two and a half thousand times less light, so a star out there would need thousands of times Sirius’s output to look as bright. Adhara looks fainter than Sirius, but far less faint than that distance would make it.
card.wonder: Moved out to Adhara’s distance, Sirius would fade below naked-eye visibility.
card.connect: Nearby Wezen and Aludra are even farther and more luminous.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: How can a star 1,600 light-years away rank among the brightest in the sky?
card.answer: It is a yellow supergiant tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun, enough to shine across that gulf.
card.glance: A creamy-yellow star in Canis Major’s hindquarters, south-east of Sirius.
card.whyHere: Wezen is a yellow supergiant more than a thousand light-years away, yet still among the brightest stars of the night.
card.see: In Canis Major’s triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara and Aludra nearby, a temperature ladder in one sweep.
card.understand: Wezen is a supergiant, one of the most luminous kinds of star, swollen and cooled in old age so that it shines yellow-white. Its distance is uncertain, because its parallax is tiny, and so is its power, which grows with the distance squared. Heavy stars like it end as supernovae, exploding when their cores give out.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 1,600 years ago, in the late Roman Empire.
card.connect: Next door, Aludra is a blue supergiant of similar power.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellowish point.

card.question: Why is Aludra’s true power so hard to pin down?
card.answer: Its distance lies somewhere between about 1,600 and 2,600 light-years, so its power, tens of thousands of times the Sun’s, comes with a wide margin.
card.glance: A blue-white point marking the end of Canis Major’s tail.
card.whyHere: Aludra is one of the most powerful stars in the winter sky, though nothing in its look says so.
card.see: Aludra is the blue-white star at the tip of the Great Dog’s tail, south-east of Sirius. Compare it with yellow Wezen to the west.
card.understand: Aludra is a blue supergiant, a hot star of the most luminous kind. Its power follows from how bright it looks and how far away it is, and at this distance the parallax is under two thousandths of an arcsecond. Since power grows with the square of the distance, a quarter’s error in distance becomes more than half in power.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 2,000 years ago, in the first years of the Roman Empire.
card.connect: Nearby, VY Canis Majoris shows where the heaviest stars head next.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Why does Gomeisa look fainter than Procyon though it is more powerful?
card.answer: Gomeisa is simply so much farther away that all its extra power cannot make up the difference, and the weaker star wins the contest of looks.
card.glance: The fainter blue-white partner of Procyon, 4° to its north-west.
card.whyHere: Gomeisa is a fast-spinning hot star with a gas disk, sitting right next to creamy Procyon.
card.see: Put Procyon and Gomeisa, in the little constellation Canis Minor, in one sweep and compare colors: Gomeisa is bluer. It is also about fourteen times farther away.
card.understand: Gomeisa is a hot blue-white star spinning fast enough to throw gas into a disk around its equator, a disk that shows up as bright hydrogen light in its spectrum. It is much more luminous than Procyon. Its distance, measured by the Hipparcos satellite, is why the stronger star looks the weaker.
card.wonder: The light you see from it left about 160 years ago, while Procyon’s left only about 11 years ago.
card.connect: Procyon, right beside it, is bright because it is close.

card.question: Can binoculars show every star in a multiple system?
card.answer: β Monocerotis keeps its secret from binoculars, looking single at 10×, and only a telescope reveals its three blue-white stars a few arcseconds apart.
card.glance: A single blue-white star in binoculars, and a famous triple in a telescope.
card.whyHere: β Monocerotis looks like a single blue-white point, but it is a showpiece for small telescopes.
card.see: β Monocerotis lies about 10° north-north-west of Sirius, in faint Monoceros. At 10× it looks single, but a small telescope at 100× splits it into a curved line of three blue-white stars.
card.understand: The three stars are only a few arcseconds apart (an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree), too close for binoculars, whose small lenses and low power cannot separate them. All three are hot blue-white stars, and they share a motion through space. The light reaching you left them about 690 years ago, and the three set out together.
card.wonder: Three stars of similar brightness in a tight line is a rare sight even in telescopes.
card.connect: σ Orionis, below Orion’s Belt, is a multiple that binoculars can split.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos show the triple; binoculars show one point.

card.question: What does a star look like as it starts shedding its outer layers?
card.answer: Much like U Monocerotis, an unsteady star rocking between deep and shallow dips as it sheds the last of its envelope.
card.glance: A yellow star in Monoceros, between Procyon and Sirius.
card.whyHere: U Monocerotis is a star near the end of its life that pulses with alternating deep and shallow dips.
card.see: U Monocerotis lies in the faint region between Procyon and Sirius. Over weeks, compare it with nearby stars: it rises and falls nearly eightfold.
card.understand: U Monocerotis is an RV Tauri star, an aging star that pulsates with alternating deep and shallow minima about every 46 days. A full cycle of one deep and one shallow dip lasts about three months. Stars like this have nearly run out of fuel and are thought to be shedding their outer layers, the step before the bare core is exposed.
card.wonder: The gas it sheds may one day glow as a planetary nebula, lit by the hot core left behind.
card.connect: ζ Geminorum shows the steadier kind of pulsating star.
